rationale.en: Semi-modals are a register- and tense-sensitive CHOICE among substitute forms for pure modals, so the correct filler ({answer}) is fixed by context, not by regular inflection.
rationale.ru: Semi-modals — это зависящий от контекста и регистра ВЫБОР формы-заменителя модального глагола, поэтому правильный вариант ({answer}) задаётся контекстом, а не регулярным словоизменением.

contexts.stem: Can has no future form, so for tomorrow we say: I ___ help you once the meeting ends.
She ___ read since she was three — a skill she has had for years. (present perfect of ability)
Students ___ use phones during the exam; the rule forbids it.
Must has no past form, so for yesterday's obligation we say: We ___ wait for an hour.
Look at those dark clouds — it ___ rain very soon. (prediction from evidence)
I haven't slept well lately; in fact I ___ sleep properly for a week. (perfect of ability)
Don't write 'can able to' — choose one. I ___ swim is correct with a semi-modal.
He ___ go now; his manager gave permission earlier. (be allowed to, needs 'be')
After 'able to' use the base verb: She was able to ___ the project on time.
Next year, with the new visa, I ___ travel freely across the EU. (future ability)
Pets ___ inside the restaurant — there's a sign on the door. (impersonal rule)
I've decided already: I ___ visit my parents next weekend. (planned future)
When the law changes, citizens ___ vote at sixteen. (future permission)
It was a tough week — I ___ work every single evening. (past obligation)
I could swim as a child, but on that one occasion I ___ swim across the whole lake. (specific past success)
Despite no training, he ___ finish the marathon — a real achievement on the day. (single success)
Smoking ___ anywhere on the premises; it's a strict company rule.
In informal British speech, 'I ___ go' means exactly 'I have to go'. (have got to)
Lucky me — last week I ___ try the new restaurant downtown. (get to = opportunity)
After 'must' use the bare infinitive: He must ___ able to defend the thesis.
The film ___ start — everyone's taking their seats right now. (very near future)
In standard modern English we say 'I don't ___ tell him', treating dare as an ordinary verb.
We've made the call: we ___ launch the product next month. (planned future)
She's got a deadline she cannot miss — she ___ submit by Friday no matter what. (have got to)
For a one-off rescue yesterday, not general ability: the lifeguard ___ pull the swimmer to shore.
'Pets may in the hotel' is wrong; a rule about a place uses: Pets ___ in the hotel.
Spoken, standard: I ___ leave early today — my supervisor okayed it. (need to)
Formal written negative of can: candidates who ___ attend should notify us in advance.
Upbeat privilege, the opposite of obligation: she ___ work from home twice a week.
External expectation, slightly British: you ___ arrive by nine, according to the schedule. (be meant to)
The dress code expects it: you ___ wear a tie to the meeting. (be supposed to)
At this hour, near-certain inevitability: there ___ be traffic on the ring road. (be bound to)
A clean probability hedge for formal writing: she ___ win the election, the polls suggest. (be likely to)
Formal 'still not', with implied expectation: the government ___ respond to the report.
Rights-based permission: full-time employees ___ twenty-five days of paid leave. (be entitled to)
Polite liberty: please ___ ask questions at any point during the talk. (be free to / feel free)
Very formal, institutional permission in a notice: visitors ___ enter the archive on weekdays.
Fixed form — 'to' plus base verb, never a participle: she has yet ___ respond.
Formal probability, the unlikely side: it ___ rain today, the forecast says. (be unlikely to)
After 'be likely' comes 'to' + base: it is likely ___ rain this afternoon.
Business-register negative of can't: we ___ process your request at this time.
C1 nuance — actual achievement, not just capacity: in the end she ___ persuade the board.
Scheduled expectation, timetable register: the train ___ arrive at ten sharp. (be due to)
Formal written instruction/arrangement: you ___ report to the director at nine. (be to + infinitive)
Unfulfilled past plan: the meeting ___ taken place last week, but it was cancelled. (was to have + V3)
Future obligation as a chain: with these cuts, you ___ explain the numbers to the board. (going to + have to)
Past habitual obligation chain: she ___ commute for hours before she moved closer. (used to + have to)
Legal drafting, codified right: each State Party ___ withdraw upon written notice. (is entitled to)
Legal drafting, pure obligation: the Licensee ___ pay the fee within thirty days. (shall)
Legal drafting, discretion: the Authority ___, in its absolute discretion, permit late filing. (may)
Failure register, three grades: he ___ secure adequate funding, falling below the target. (fell short of)
Formal success, V-ing complement: the team ___ reducing latency by half. (succeeded in)
Academic hedging — presumption: the transaction ___ have taken place before the audit. (is presumed to)
Academic hedging — judgement: the evidence ___ be sufficient for publication. (is deemed to)
Moral semi-modal with evaluative weight, stronger than neutral should: one ___ tell the truth here.
Recognise but don't write it in standard prose — this is dialectal (Southern US/Scots): 'I ___ help you.'
Unfulfilled plan needs 'have' + participle, not the bare verb: the project ___ been completed by December.
Formal arrangement / news register: the ambassador ___ meet the prime minister on Tuesday. (be to)
Negotiated discretion in a treaty exception clause: nothing herein ___ be construed as requiring disclosure. (shall)
Don't stack a modal onto its own semi-modal twin: he ___ secure funding, not 'can be able to'.
